topics.h: Ask five people what 'a better life' means and you may get five different answers — and some of them may even clash!
p: Development means progress, but people do not all want the same things. Each person's development goals depend on their life situation.
A landless rural labourer may want more days of work and better wages; a prosperous farmer may want higher prices for crops; a girl in a city may want the same freedom as her brother.
Goals can conflict: a big dam may give electricity to industries and cities, but it may submerge villages and force families to move. Development for one group can mean loss for another.
People want more income, but they also seek non-material things: equal treatment, freedom, security, respect from others and friendship.

Some things money cannot buy for one person alone: a pollution-free environment, medicines that are not adulterated, or protection from infectious diseases. These usually need the whole community or the government to act together.

ex.q: Think it through: Arjun gets two job offers. Job A pays ₹5,000 more per month but is in a faraway city with no job security. Job B pays a little less, is close to his family and is permanent. What should he consider?
st: Income matters: Job A gives more money each month.
Non-income factors also matter: job security, time with family, a safe working atmosphere and chances to learn.
Job B offers security and family support, which money alone cannot buy.
So the choice depends on Arjun's own goals — there is no single answer that is right for everyone.
ex.a: Both income and non-income goals matter; the 'better' job depends on what Arjun values most.

topics.rl: When your family discusses moving to a new city for a job, they think about salary, but also schools, safety, distance from grandparents and the neighbourhood — that is development thinking in action.

rv.summary: Different people have different development goals, depending on their life situation, and these goals can conflict. People want more income, but also non-material things like freedom, equality, security and respect.

topics.t: Per capita income: comparing countries and states
topics.h: A cricket team's total runs don't tell you how good each batter is — and a country's total income doesn't tell you how well-off each person is!
p: Income is the most common way to compare countries: a country with more income is usually thought to be more developed, because people can buy more of what they need.
Total income is not a fair comparison, because countries have different populations. So we use average income: total income of the country ÷ its total population.

Average income is also called per capita income ('per head'). The World Bank's World Development Report uses per capita income to classify countries; it places India among low middle income countries.
An average can hide inequality: two countries can have the same average income, but in one everyone earns about the same while in the other a few are very rich and most are poor.
So per capita income is useful but incomplete — it says nothing about how income is shared or about health and education.

ex.q: Think it through: Village Sundarpur has 5 families earning ₹9,000, ₹11,000, ₹10,000, ₹9,500 and ₹10,500 a month. Village Rampur has 5 families earning ₹1,000, ₹1,000, ₹1,000, ₹1,000 and ₹46,000. Compare them.
st: Both averages are equal, but in Rampur four families earn only ₹1,000 each.
Sundarpur's income is shared far more equally, so most people would prefer to live there.
ex.a: Same average (₹10,000), but Sundarpur is more equal — averages hide how income is distributed.

topics.rl: If a class's average marks are 70, it could be that everyone scored about 70 — or that some scored 100 and some scored 40. You need more than the average to know the full story.

rv.summary: Countries are compared by average or per capita income, which is total income ÷ total population. It is useful, but an average can hide inequality and says nothing about health or education.

topics.h: Would you rather live where people earn a little more — or where babies survive, children study and the hospital is close by?
p: Infant Mortality Rate (IMR): the number of children who die before the age of one year for every 1000 live births in that year. Literacy rate: the proportion of literate people in the 7 years and above age group. Net attendance ratio: children aged 14 and 15 attending school as a percentage of all children of that age.

A state with lower per capita income can still do better in health and education. The textbook shows Kerala with a low infant mortality rate and high literacy because it has adequate basic health and education facilities.

Many important needs are best met by public facilities provided collectively: schools, health centres, and ration shops of the Public Distribution System. Collective provision is often cheaper and reaches more people.

The UNDP's Human Development Report compares countries by their educational levels, health status and per capita income. Its Human Development Index (HDI) uses life expectancy at birth, mean years of schooling, expected years of schooling and gross national income per capita.

Sustainability: development should continue for future generations too. Groundwater is a renewable resource refilled by rain, but it gets used up if we pump it faster than it is refilled. Crude oil is non-renewable — its stock is limited and will run out.

ex.q: Think it through: State X has a higher per capita income than State Y, but State X's IMR is 30 while State Y's IMR is 6. Which state has better health conditions, and why might this happen?
st: IMR counts infant deaths per 1000 live births, so a lower IMR is better.
State Y loses 6 babies out of every 1000, State X loses 30 — State Y is far better.
Money in people's pockets cannot by itself buy vaccination drives, clean water or nearby health centres.
State Y has probably invested in public health and education facilities.
ex.a: State Y, because it has a much lower IMR; good public health facilities matter, not just income.

topics.rl: When an anganwadi in your area gives free check-ups and nutrition to small children, or a government school gives midday meals, that is public provision improving human development.

rv.summary: Development is also measured by health and education, using IMR, literacy rate and net attendance ratio. UNDP's HDI combines health, education and income, and sustainable development protects resources for future generations.

topics.t: Primary, secondary and tertiary sectors and GDP
topics.h: Your morning cup of chai passes through all three sectors of the economy before it reaches your hands!
p: Primary sector: producing goods by directly using natural resources — agriculture, dairy, fishing, forestry and mining. It is also called the agriculture and related sector.
Secondary sector: changing natural products into other forms through manufacturing — sugar from sugarcane, cloth from cotton, bricks from clay. It is also called the industrial sector.

Tertiary sector: activities that support the other two and produce services rather than goods — transport, storage, communication, banking and trade, plus services of teachers, doctors, lawyers and IT workers. It is also called the service sector.
The sectors depend on each other: a farmer needs transport and a market, and a textile mill needs cotton from farmers.

Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year. Only final goods are counted, because the value of intermediate goods (like cotton used to make cloth) is already included in the final good's value — counting both would be double counting.

ex.q: Think it through: A farmer sells sugarcane worth ₹40 to a mill. The mill makes sugar and sells it for ₹70 to a sweet shop. The sweet shop uses it to make jalebis and sells them to customers for ₹200. How much is added to GDP?
st: Sugarcane and sugar are intermediate goods here — they are used up in making something else.
The jalebis sold to customers are the final good, worth ₹200.
The ₹200 price already includes the value of the sugar and sugarcane used.
Adding 40 + 70 + 200 = ₹310 would count the sugarcane and sugar more than once.
ex.a: ₹200 — only the value of the final good is counted.

topics.rl: The tea leaves are plucked in Assam's gardens (primary), processed and packed in a factory (secondary), and carried by trucks and sold at your local kirana shop (tertiary).

rv.summary: The economy has three sectors: primary (using natural resources), secondary (manufacturing) and tertiary (services). They depend on each other. GDP is the value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a year.

topics.h: Five people working on a field that needs only three — everyone looks busy, but is everyone really needed?
p: In the early stages of development, the primary sector was the most important. As farming improved and produced more food, people moved to manufacturing and the secondary sector became most important. In developed countries today, the tertiary sector is the most important.
In India, production has grown in all three sectors, but most in the tertiary sector, which has become the largest producing sector, replacing the primary sector.

Reasons for tertiary growth: basic services like hospitals, schools, post offices, police, courts and banks are needed; growing farms and factories need more transport, trade and storage; rising incomes create demand for services like eating out, tourism and private schools; new IT-based services have grown fast. But many tertiary workers, like small shopkeepers and repair workers, still earn very little.

Jobs did not shift the same way: the primary sector is still the largest employer in India, even though its share in GDP is much smaller. The secondary and tertiary sectors have not created enough jobs.

Disguised unemployment (underemployment): more people work than are needed, so if some leave, output does not fall. It is common in farming and also among urban casual workers who have work only part of the time.

More jobs can come from irrigation, rural roads, storage and cheap credit, agro-processing units, tourism, health and education. The textbook also describes MGNREGA 2005, a law that guaranteed 100 days of work in a year to rural people who needed and could do work, with an unemployment allowance if work was not given. Update: in December 2025 a new law, the Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-G RAM G), was passed to replace MGNREGA from 1 July 2026; it guarantees 125 days of wage work in a year. For your exam, learn MGNREGA as the textbook describes it.

ex.q: Think it through: Meena's family of 5 works on a small 2-hectare farm. The farm needs only 3 workers. Two family members find jobs in a nearby town and production stays the same. What does this show?
st: Before, 5 people worked but only 3 were really needed.
When 2 left, output did not fall, so their labour was adding nothing extra.
This is disguised unemployment: people appear employed but are not fully productive.
The 2 members can now add to the family income from the town, so the family is better off.
ex.a: 2 members were disguisedly unemployed; moving them to other work raises total income.

topics.rl: On a city street, many painters and plumbers wait at a chowk every morning for daily work; many get work only on some days — another form of underemployment.

rv.summary: In India the tertiary sector has become the largest producer, but the primary sector is still the largest employer. Many farm workers are disguisedly unemployed, and schemes like MGNREGA aim to create more jobs.

topics.h: Two people both work 8 hours a day — one gets paid leave and a pension, the other can lose the job tomorrow. What's the difference?
p: Organised sector: enterprises or places of work with regular terms of employment. They are registered by the government and must follow laws such as the Factories Act, Minimum Wages Act, Payment of Gratuity Act and Shops and Establishments Act. (Update: since 21 November 2025 the Factories Act, Minimum Wages Act, Payment of Gratuity Act and many other central labour laws have been combined into four new Labour Codes; the idea of the organised sector stays the same.)

Organised-sector workers get job security, fixed working hours, extra pay for overtime, paid leave, payment during holidays, provident fund, gratuity, medical benefits and often a pension after retirement.

Unorganised sector: small, scattered units largely outside government control. Rules exist but are often not followed. Jobs are low-paid and irregular, with no overtime pay, paid leave or sick leave, and workers can be removed without reason.

Many people work in the unorganised sector: in villages — landless labourers, small and marginal farmers, sharecroppers and artisans; in towns — casual construction workers, street vendors, head-load workers, garment workers in small units and rag pickers.
Unorganised workers need protection: the government can fix minimum wages and working hours, and help small units with cheap loans, raw materials and marketing.

ex.q: Think it through: Sunil works in a registered car-parts factory with a written contract, paid leave and provident fund. His cousin Raju works at a small roadside workshop, is paid in cash daily and gets nothing when he falls ill. Which sector does each belong to?
st: Sunil's job has regular terms, is registered and gives benefits like paid leave and provident fund.
These are features of the organised sector.
Raju's job is irregular, has no leave or security and follows no formal rules.
These are features of the unorganised sector.
ex.a: Sunil — organised sector; Raju — unorganised sector.

topics.rl: The person who sells bhutta near your school, the helper at a small dhaba and the daily-wage worker building a house are mostly in the unorganised sector; a bank clerk or a railway engineer is in the organised sector.

rv.summary: The organised sector has registered units with regular jobs and benefits like paid leave, provident fund and overtime pay. The unorganised sector has small, scattered units with low-paid, irregular jobs and no security, so its workers need protection.

topics.h: The train you ride and the biscuit you munch on it are made by two very different kinds of owners!
p: Sectors can also be classified by who owns the assets. In the public sector, the government owns most of the assets and provides the services, like the Indian Railways and post offices.
In the private sector, assets are owned and services delivered by private individuals or companies.
The private sector's main motive is to earn profits. The public sector's aim is not just profit but public welfare; the government raises money through taxes to pay for its services.

Some things need huge spending that the private sector will not provide at a reasonable cost: roads, bridges, railways, harbours, generating electricity and irrigation through dams. It is also hard to collect money from thousands of users, so the government provides these.

The government also supports private activity — for example, it sells electricity at low rates to industries, and buys wheat and rice from farmers at a fair price, stores them and sells them at lower prices through ration shops. It also has a duty to provide health and education facilities for all.

ex.q: Think it through: Why would a private company not want to build a long bridge connecting a few villages across a river?
st: Building a bridge costs a huge amount of money.
Collecting a fee from every villager who walks or cycles across would be very hard.
The private company could not earn enough profit, so it would not invest.
The government, which aims at public welfare and collects taxes, can build it for everyone.
ex.a: Because it is too costly and unprofitable for a private company; the government builds it for public welfare.

topics.rl: When your family buys rice and wheat at a lower price from the local ration shop, you see the government supporting both farmers and consumers.

rv.summary: By ownership, the economy has a public sector (government owns assets, aims at public welfare, funded by taxes) and a private sector (private owners, aims at profit). The government provides costly facilities like roads, dams and railways, and supports farmers and consumers.

topics.t: Money as a medium of exchange
topics.h: Imagine trying to buy a samosa by offering the shopkeeper a pair of socks — and he wants a cricket ball instead!
p: In a barter system, goods are exchanged directly for goods. It needs a double coincidence of wants: what one person wants to sell must be exactly what the other wants to buy, and the other way round.
Money acts as a medium of exchange — an in-between item in every exchange. A person sells goods for money and uses that money to buy what she needs, so double coincidence is no longer needed.
Many things have served as money: in early times Indians used grains and cattle; later came metallic coins of gold, silver and copper; today we use paper notes and coins.

Modern currency has no use of its own; it is accepted because the government authorises it. In India, the Reserve Bank of India issues currency notes on behalf of the central government, and by law the rupee cannot be refused for settling payments in India.

People also keep money as deposits in banks and earn interest. Demand deposits can be withdrawn whenever needed. A cheque is a paper instructing the bank to pay a specific amount from the account to the person named on it. Because demand deposits are widely accepted for payment, they share the essential features of money.

Banks keep only a small part of their deposits as cash and lend most of the rest. They charge a higher interest rate on loans than they pay on deposits; this difference is the main source of a bank's income.

ex.q: Think it through: A shoemaker in Agra wants wheat. A wheat farmer wants cloth, not shoes. Can they trade by barter? How does money help?
st: The shoemaker wants wheat, but the farmer does not want shoes.
So there is no double coincidence of wants and barter fails.
With money, the shoemaker sells shoes to anyone who wants them and gets money.
He then pays the farmer money for wheat, and the farmer uses it to buy cloth.
ex.a: Barter fails without double coincidence; money as a medium of exchange solves the problem.

topics.rl: When your parent pays the vegetable seller by cheque, card or a phone payment from a bank account, the money moves out of a bank deposit — deposits work just like cash.

rv.summary: Barter needs a double coincidence of wants. Money solves this by acting as a medium of exchange. Modern currency is accepted because the government authorises it, and bank demand deposits also work like money.

topics.h: A loan can be a ladder that helps you climb — or a pit that is hard to climb out of!
p: Credit (a loan) is an agreement in which the lender supplies the borrower with money, goods or services in return for a promise of future payment.

Credit can help: a potter borrows before Diwali to buy clay and colours, sells many diyas, repays and still earns a profit. Credit can also hurt: if a farmer's crop fails, she cannot repay and may have to sell land or borrow again. This is a debt trap.

Terms of credit include the interest rate, collateral, documentation and mode of repayment. Collateral is an asset the borrower owns — land, a building, a vehicle, livestock or bank deposits — kept as a guarantee; if the loan is not repaid, the lender can sell it.

Formal sources are banks and cooperatives. The Reserve Bank of India supervises them: it checks that banks keep enough cash, makes sure they lend to small farmers, small industries and small borrowers too, and collects information on whom they lend to and at what rate.

Informal sources are moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives and friends. No organisation supervises them, so they may charge very high interest and use unfair ways to get money back. Higher interest means a bigger share of the borrower's earnings goes in repayment.

Rich households take most of their loans from formal sources, while poor households depend largely on informal sources — they often lack collateral and documents. So formal credit must expand, especially in rural areas, and reach the poor.

ex.q: Think it through: Ravi borrows ₹10,000 for one year. A moneylender charges 5% per month; a bank charges 12% per year. How much more interest does he pay the moneylender?
st: Moneylender: 5% of ₹10,000 = ₹500 per month; for 12 months = ₹6,000.
Bank: 12% of ₹10,000 for one year = ₹1,200.
The high informal interest eats a large part of Ravi's earnings.
ex.a: ₹4,800 more — formal credit is much cheaper.

topics.rl: When a farmer in your village takes a crop loan from a bank or a cooperative society instead of a moneylender, she saves a lot on interest.

rv.summary: Credit is a loan given now for a promise of future payment. Its terms are interest rate, collateral, documentation and repayment. Formal sources (banks, cooperatives) are supervised by the RBI and are cheaper; informal sources are not supervised and often charge high interest.

topics.h: What if twenty neighbours could become their own little bank? That's the idea behind a Self-Help Group!
p: A Self-Help Group (SHG) typically has 15–20 members, usually women from the same neighbourhood, who meet and save regularly.
Members can take small loans from the group's own savings, at an interest rate lower than the moneylender's.

After a year or two, if the group saves regularly, it becomes eligible for a bank loan. The loan is sanctioned in the group's name and is meant to create self-employment — for example, to buy sewing machines, cattle or raw materials.

The group decides who gets a loan, how much, the interest and repayment. The group is responsible for repayment, and members follow up if someone does not repay. So banks are willing to lend to SHGs even without collateral.
SHGs help women become financially self-reliant, and their regular meetings let members discuss issues like health, nutrition and domestic violence.

Cooperatives also help: members such as farmers or weavers pool their resources; a farmers' cooperative accepts deposits from members, uses them as collateral to get a large bank loan, and lends to members. In Bangladesh, the Grameen Bank, started by Muhammad Yunus, has given credit to the poor at reasonable rates; Yunus and the Grameen Bank received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2006.

ex.q: Think it through: Lakshmi has no land to offer as collateral. She wants ₹15,000 to buy a sewing machine. How can an SHG help her?
st: Lakshmi joins an SHG of 18 women who save a small amount every month.
She can first borrow a small amount from the group's savings at low interest.
Once the group has saved regularly for a year or two, the bank gives it a loan without collateral.
The group lends Lakshmi ₹15,000; she stitches clothes, earns and repays in instalments.
ex.a: The SHG gives her access to cheap credit without collateral, helping her become self-employed.

topics.rl: In many states, women's SHGs make pickles, papad, agarbattis or handicrafts and sell them at local melas — earning, saving and supporting one another.

topics.h: Your football may be designed in one country, stitched in another and sold in a third — all by one company!
p: Until about the middle of the 20th century, production was organised mostly within countries. What crossed borders were raw materials, food and finished goods. Colonies like India exported raw materials and food and imported finished goods.

A Multinational Corporation (MNC) is a company that owns or controls production in more than one nation. MNCs set up offices and factories where they can get cheaper labour and other resources, to lower costs and earn more profit.
MNCs choose places that are close to markets, have skilled and unskilled labour at low cost, have other factors of production available, and have government policies that look after their interests.
Investment is money spent to buy assets such as land, buildings, machines and equipment. Investment made by MNCs is called foreign investment.

MNCs spread production by: setting up production jointly with local companies (bringing money for new machines and the latest technology); buying up local companies, which is the most common route; and placing orders with small producers, for example for garments, footwear and sports goods, which the MNC then sells under its own brand name.
Foreign trade connects markets: producers can sell beyond their own country, and buyers get more choice. For example, toys made in China are sold in Indian markets.

ex.q: Think it through: A foreign company that makes mobile phones wants to open a factory in Asia. Why might it choose a city in India?
st: India has a very large market of buyers close by.
It has many skilled engineers and workers at relatively low wages.
If roads, ports, power and government policies are favourable, costs fall further.
Lower costs and a big market mean higher profits for the MNC.
ex.a: Because of a large nearby market, low-cost skilled labour and supportive facilities and policies.

topics.rl: Look at the label on your school bag, shoes or toy: 'Made in India' for a foreign brand, or 'Made in China' on a toy sold in your local market, shows production spread across countries.

rv.summary: An MNC owns or controls production in more than one nation. It sets up where labour is cheap and markets are near, to cut costs and raise profits, through joint production, buying local companies or placing orders. Foreign trade gives buyers more choice.

topics.h: A call centre worker in Bengaluru can help a customer on another continent at midnight — welcome to a connected world!
p: Globalisation is the process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries, mainly through more foreign trade and more foreign investment by MNCs. Goods, services, investments and technology move across countries; the movement of people is still limited.

Technology made it possible: faster and cheaper transport (containers carry goods on ships, trains, planes and trucks), and information and communication technology — telecommunications, computers and the internet. A magazine can be designed in Delhi and printed in Mumbai; call centres serve customers abroad.

A trade barrier is a restriction on trade set by the government, such as a tax on imports or a limit on how much can be imported. It lets the government decide which goods and how much of them enter the country.
After independence, India put barriers on foreign trade and foreign investment to protect its young industries from foreign competition.

Around 1991, India made big changes in its economic policy and removed barriers on trade and investment to a large extent. Removing barriers or restrictions set by the government is called liberalisation. Indian producers now had to compete with foreign producers, which was expected to push them to improve quality.

ex.q: Think it through: The government puts a heavy tax on imported toys. What happens to toy prices and to Indian toy makers?
st: The import tax makes foreign toys costlier in Indian shops.
Fewer people buy imported toys.
Indian toy makers face less competition and sell more.
This is how a trade barrier protects domestic producers — and removing it (liberalisation) brings more competition.
ex.a: Imported toys become costlier, so Indian makers are protected; the tax is a trade barrier.

topics.rl: Video calls with relatives working in the Gulf, or an online order shipped from another country, show how technology links people and markets across the world.

rv.summary: Globalisation is rapid integration of countries through foreign trade and foreign investment, helped by faster transport and information technology. India had trade barriers after independence, but around 1991 it liberalised by removing many of them.
focus: Define globalisation and what moves freely vs what is limited
Technology that made globalisation possible
Define a trade barrier and why India used them after independence
Liberalisation around 1991 and its effect on Indian producers
remember: Globalisation: rapid integration or interconnection between countries
Movement of people between countries is still limited
Trade barrier: a government restriction on trade, e.g. a tax on imports
Liberalisation: removing barriers or restrictions set by the government (India, around 1991)
traps: Don't think people move as freely as goods and investment
Barriers after independence were to protect Indian producers, not to help foreign firms
Liberalisation increases competition; it does not reduce it

topics.t: WTO, impact of globalisation and fair globalisation
topics.h: Globalisation is like a big cricket tournament — great if the rules are fair for every team, not just the strongest!
p: The World Trade Organisation (WTO) aims to liberalise international trade. Started at the initiative of developed countries, it sets rules for international trade and checks that they are obeyed.

Critics say WTO rules have been unfair: developed countries have kept their own trade barriers while pushing developing countries to remove theirs. The textbook's example: the US government gives large sums of money to its farmers, so they can sell farm products abroad at very low prices, which hurts farmers in developing countries.

Who gained in India: well-off consumers (more choice, better quality, lower prices); MNCs increased investment in mobile phones, automobiles, electronics, soft drinks, fast food and banking in cities; local companies supplying MNCs; some large Indian companies became MNCs themselves; IT service companies got new opportunities.

Who faced difficulties: many small producers — for example of batteries, capacitors, plastics, toys, tyres, dairy products and vegetable oil — faced tough competition and some shut down. Many workers now get only temporary, flexible jobs with long hours and little security.

To attract foreign companies, the government set up Special Economic Zones (SEZs) with world-class facilities — electricity, water, roads, transport, storage, recreation and education. According to the textbook, companies setting up units in SEZs do not pay taxes for an initial period of five years.

Fair globalisation creates opportunities for all and shares the benefits better. The government can make sure labour laws are followed, support small producers, use trade and investment barriers if needed, and join other developing countries to bargain for fairer WTO rules. People's organisations and campaigns can also make a difference.

ex.q: Think it through: Cheap imported toys flood the market. Small toy makers in a town are losing business. What could make globalisation fairer for them?
st: Consumers gain from cheaper toys, but the small producers lose income.
The government could help small makers improve quality and lower costs with cheap credit and better technology.
If needed, it could use a trade barrier, such as an import tax, to give them time to become competitive.
It could also negotiate at the WTO for fairer rules for developing countries.
ex.a: Support small producers, use barriers where needed, and bargain for fair rules — so benefits are shared by all.

topics.rl: Wooden toys from Channapatna in Karnataka and Etikoppaka in Andhra Pradesh compete with imported toys; support for such small producers is part of making globalisation fair.

rv.summary: The WTO, started at the initiative of developed countries, aims to liberalise trade, but its rules are often unfair to developing countries. In India, well-off consumers and many companies gained, while small producers and workers faced difficulties. Fair globalisation shares benefits with all.
focus: Aim of the WTO and why its rules are called unfair
Who gained and who lost from globalisation in India
Special Economic Zones and their facilities
Steps towards fair globalisation
remember: WTO aims to liberalise international trade; started at the initiative of developed countries
US farm subsidies let US farmers sell cheaply, hurting farmers in developing countries
SEZ units pay no taxes for an initial period of five years (textbook)
Fair globalisation creates opportunities for all and shares the benefits better

qa.q: Which development goal would a landless rural labourer most likely have?
qa.a: More days of work and better wages
qa.e: A landless labourer does not own land or a factory; he depends on wages, so more work and better pay are his main goals.

qa.q: A dam will give electricity to cities but will submerge several villages. What does this show about development?
qa.a: Development goals can conflict: one group's gain may be another's loss
qa.e: City users and industries gain power, while villagers lose their homes and land, so their goals clash.

qa.q: Which of these is a non-material development goal?
qa.a: Being treated with respect and equality
qa.e: Respect and equal treatment cannot be bought or measured in money, so they are non-material goals.

qa.q: Which of these is hardest for one family to buy with its own money?
qa.a: A pollution-free environment
qa.e: Clean air and water depend on what everyone around does, so they need community or government action, not one family's spending.

qa.q: Dengue spreads through mosquitoes breeding in stagnant water. What is the most effective protection for a colony?
qa.a: Everyone together clearing stagnant water across the whole colony
qa.e: Mosquitoes fly from house to house, so protection works only when the whole community acts together.

qa.q: Priya is choosing between two jobs with equal pay. Which factor is a non-income reason to prefer one job?
qa.a: A safe working atmosphere and job security
qa.e: Safety and security are not about money but still make a job better. The other options are all about income.

qa.q: Why do different people have different notions of development?
qa.a: Because people's life situations, needs and hopes are different
qa.e: People in different situations — farmers, workers, students, business owners — need and hope for different things.

qa.q: Which pair shows conflicting development goals?
qa.a: An industrialist wants a new factory on farmland; farmers want to keep farming that land
qa.e: The same land cannot be used for both, so the industrialist's goal and the farmers' goal clash.

qa.q: How is per capita income of a country calculated?
qa.a: Total income ÷ total population
qa.e: Per capita means 'per head', so we divide the total income by the whole population.

qa.q: Five families in a village earn ₹10,000, ₹12,000, ₹8,000, ₹30,000 and ₹40,000 a month. What is the average income per family?
qa.e: Total = ₹1,00,000. Divided among 5 families, the average is ₹20,000.

qa.q: Why is total income NOT a useful way to compare two countries?
qa.a: Because countries have different populations, so total income tells little about what an average person earns
qa.e: A big country may have a huge total income but also a huge population, so we must look at income per person.

qa.q: Which report classifies countries mainly by their per capita income?
qa.a: World Development Report of the World Bank
qa.e: The World Bank's World Development Report uses per capita income. The UNDP's report uses the Human Development Index instead.

qa.q: In the World Bank's classification, in which group does India fall?
qa.a: Low middle income
qa.e: India's per capita income places it among the low middle income countries.

qa.q: An island has a total yearly income of ₹90,00,000 and 300 people. What is its per capita income?
Country P and Country Q have the same average income. In P, everyone earns about the same; in Q, one person is very rich and the rest are poor. Where would most people prefer to live?
qa.a: Country P, because income is shared more equally
qa.e: With equal averages, the country with fairer distribution gives most people a better income.

qa.q: What is the main weakness of using only per capita income to measure development?
qa.a: It does not show how income is distributed or how healthy and educated people are
qa.e: Per capita income is an average; it hides inequality and says nothing about health, education or other facilities.

qa.q: What does the Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) measure?
qa.a: Number of children who die before age one per 1000 live births in a year
qa.e: IMR counts deaths of babies before their first birthday out of every 1000 live births in that year.

qa.q: Literacy rate measures the proportion of literate people in which age group?
qa.a: 7 years and above
qa.e: Literacy rate is calculated for the population aged 7 years and above.

qa.q: In a district, there were 4000 live births in a year and 60 of these babies died before their first birthday. What is the IMR?
qa.e: IMR is per 1000 live births: 60 ÷ 4000 × 1000 = 15.

qa.q: Which organisation publishes the Human Development Report?
qa.a: UNDP
qa.e: The Human Development Report is published by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).

qa.q: Which of these is NOT used in calculating the Human Development Index?
qa.a: Number of cars per family
qa.e: HDI combines health (life expectancy), education (years of schooling) and income. Cars owned are not part of it.

qa.q: According to the textbook, why does Kerala have a low infant mortality rate?
qa.a: Because it has adequate provision of basic health and educational facilities
qa.e: Kerala's good basic health and education facilities, not just income, keep its IMR low.

qa.q: Groundwater is a renewable resource. Why can it still run short?
qa.a: Because it is used faster than rain can refill it
qa.e: A renewable resource is refilled by nature, but if we pump out more than is refilled, it gets overused and falls.

qa.q: What does 'sustainable development' mean?
qa.a: Development that meets today's needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs
qa.e: Sustainability means development should continue for future generations, so resources and the environment must be protected.

qa.q: Fishing belongs to which sector of the economy?
qa.a: Primary sector
qa.e: Fishing directly uses a natural resource, so it is a primary sector activity.

qa.q: Making sugar from sugarcane is an activity of which sector?
qa.a: Secondary sector
qa.e: Sugarcane, a natural product, is changed into sugar through manufacturing — a secondary sector activity.

qa.q: Why is the tertiary sector also called the service sector?
qa.a: Because it produces services rather than goods
qa.e: Transport, banking, teaching and trade do not produce goods themselves; they provide services.

qa.q: Which is the correct meaning of GDP?
qa.a: The value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year
qa.e: GDP measures the value of final goods and services produced within the country in one year.

qa.q: A farmer sells cotton for ₹50 to a mill, the mill sells yarn for ₹80 to a weaver, and the weaver sells cloth to customers for ₹150. What value is added to GDP?
qa.e: Only the final good, the cloth worth ₹150, is counted. Its price already includes the cotton and yarn.

qa.q: Which of these is an intermediate good?
qa.a: Flour bought by a biscuit factory to make biscuits
qa.e: The flour is used up in making biscuits, so it is an intermediate good. The others are final goods or services used by consumers.

qa.q: Why are only final goods counted in GDP?
qa.a: Because the value of intermediate goods is already included in the final value, so counting them would be double counting
qa.e: The price of the final good already covers the intermediate goods used to make it.

qa.q: If all truck drivers go on strike, farmers cannot send vegetables to cities. What does this show?
qa.a: The three sectors depend on each other
qa.e: Farmers (primary) need transport (tertiary) to reach markets, so the sectors are interdependent.

qa.q: Which sector has become the largest producing sector in India?
qa.a: Tertiary sector
qa.e: Production grew fastest in the tertiary sector, which replaced the primary sector as the largest producer.

qa.q: Which sector still employs the largest number of workers in India?
qa.a: Primary sector
qa.e: Most workers are still in the primary sector, mainly agriculture, although its share in GDP is much smaller.

qa.q: Kamla's family of 5 works on a plot that needs only 3 workers. How many family members are disguisedly unemployed?
qa.e: Only 3 are needed, so 5 − 3 = 2 members are not really adding to output.

qa.q: Which is a reason for the growth of the tertiary sector in India?
qa.a: Rising incomes increase demand for services like restaurants, tourism and private schools
qa.e: As incomes rise, people spend more on services, which helps the tertiary sector grow.

qa.q: What is disguised unemployment?
qa.a: When more people work than needed, so some are not really productive
qa.e: In disguised unemployment, everyone seems to be working, but removing some workers would not reduce output.

qa.q: Historically, as countries developed, which sector became the most important after the primary sector?
qa.a: Secondary sector
qa.e: Better farming freed people to work in manufacturing, so the secondary sector became most important next; the tertiary sector rose later.

qa.q: As described in the textbook, MGNREGA 2005 guaranteed rural people who needed work how many days of employment in a year?
qa.a: 100 days
qa.e: The textbook explains that MGNREGA 2005 guaranteed 100 days of employment in a year, and an unemployment allowance if work was not provided. (Update: from 1 July 2026 MGNREGA is replaced by the VB-G RAM G Act, 2025, which guarantees 125 days.)

qa.q: Which step would best create more jobs in a village where farmers grow only one crop a year?
qa.a: Building wells or canals for irrigation
qa.e: Irrigation lets farmers grow a second crop, which needs more workers and creates more jobs.

qa.q: Which of these is a feature of the organised sector?
qa.a: Paid leave and provident fund
qa.e: Organised-sector workers get benefits such as paid leave, provident fund and job security.

qa.q: Organised-sector enterprises are those that are:
qa.a: Registered by the government and follow its rules and regulations
qa.e: The key feature is registration and following laws; a privately owned firm can also be in the organised sector.

qa.q: A woman sells vegetables from a handcart on the street. She has no fixed income and no leave. Which sector is she in?
qa.a: Unorganised sector
qa.e: Her work is irregular, unregistered and without benefits, so it is in the unorganised sector.

qa.q: Rakesh works overtime in a registered factory. What is he entitled to under organised-sector rules?
qa.a: Extra payment for the overtime
qa.e: In the organised sector, employers must pay extra for overtime work.

qa.q: Why do unorganised-sector workers need protection?
qa.a: Because their jobs are low-paid, irregular and without security
qa.e: Unorganised workers face low pay, irregular work and no job security, so they need support and protection.

qa.q: The textbook lists laws about workers that organised-sector enterprises must follow. Which of these is one of them?
qa.a: Minimum Wages Act
qa.e: The Minimum Wages Act, like the Factories Act and the Payment of Gratuity Act, sets rules about workers' pay and conditions. The other laws deal with information, wildlife and elections. (Since November 2025 these labour laws have been combined into four Labour Codes.)

qa.q: Which group of workers is mostly found in the unorganised sector in rural areas?
qa.a: Landless labourers, sharecroppers and artisans
qa.e: Landless labourers, small farmers, sharecroppers and artisans usually have irregular work and no benefits.

qa.q: Which government step would most directly help small units in the unorganised sector?
qa.a: Providing cheap loans, raw materials and help in marketing
qa.e: Cheap credit, raw materials and marketing help let small units earn more and survive.

qa.q: On what basis are sectors classified as public and private?
qa.a: Who owns the assets and delivers the services
qa.e: Public and private sectors are classified by ownership.

qa.q: Indian Railways belongs to which sector?
qa.a: Public sector
qa.e: The government owns and runs the Indian Railways, so it is in the public sector.

qa.q: What is the main motive of the private sector?
qa.a: Earning profit
qa.e: Private owners invest to earn profits.

qa.q: How does the government mainly raise money for public sector services?
qa.a: Through taxes
qa.e: The government collects taxes from people and businesses to pay for public services.

qa.q: Why does the government usually build roads, bridges and dams?
qa.a: Because they need huge spending and it is hard to collect money from all users, so private firms won't provide them at a reasonable cost
qa.e: These projects cost a lot and are hard to charge every user for, so the government provides them for public welfare.

qa.q: The government buys wheat from farmers at a fair price and sells it at a lower price through ration shops. Whom does this help?
qa.a: Both farmers and poor consumers
qa.e: Farmers get a fair price and poor consumers get cheaper grain; the government bears part of the cost.

qa.q: A chain of hospitals is owned by a group of private shareholders. Which sector does it belong to?
qa.a: Private sector
qa.e: Ownership by private shareholders puts it in the private sector; a hospital's activity is in the tertiary sector.

qa.q: Dividing the economy into organised and unorganised sectors is based on:
qa.a: Conditions of employment
qa.e: Organised and unorganised sectors differ in terms of employment — rules, security and benefits.

qa.q: What does 'double coincidence of wants' mean?
qa.a: What one person wants to sell is exactly what the other wants to buy, and the other way round
qa.e: In barter, each person must want exactly what the other is offering for the exchange to happen.

qa.q: How does money solve the problem of double coincidence of wants?
qa.a: By acting as a medium of exchange that everyone accepts
qa.e: A seller accepts money and spends it on what she needs later, so the two people need not want each other's goods.

qa.q: Who issues currency notes in India?
qa.a: Reserve Bank of India, on behalf of the central government
qa.e: The Reserve Bank of India issues currency notes on behalf of the central government.

qa.q: Why is a ₹100 note accepted as money even though the paper itself is of little use?
qa.a: Because the government authorises it as a medium of payment
qa.e: Modern currency is accepted because it is authorised by the government; by law, the rupee cannot be refused in India.

qa.q: Why are some bank deposits called demand deposits?
qa.a: Because they can be withdrawn whenever the depositor wants
qa.e: Money in demand deposits can be taken out on demand, which is why they can be used for payments like cash.

qa.q: What is a cheque?
qa.a: A paper instructing the bank to pay a specific amount from a person's account to the person named on it
qa.e: A cheque tells the bank to transfer money from the account holder to the named person.

qa.q: What do banks do with most of the money people deposit?
qa.a: Lend it out as loans, keeping only a small part as cash
qa.e: Banks keep a small portion as cash for withdrawals and use most deposits to give loans.

qa.q: A bank pays 5% yearly interest on deposits and charges 9% yearly on loans. If it lends ₹1,00,000 of deposits for a year, how much does it earn from the difference?
qa.e: It earns ₹9,000 from the borrower and pays ₹5,000 to depositors, so it keeps ₹4,000.

qa.q: What is credit?
qa.a: An agreement in which a lender supplies money, goods or services in return for a promise of future payment
qa.e: Credit is a loan given now on the promise that it will be repaid later.

qa.q: Which of these could serve as collateral for a loan?
qa.a: The borrower's land or house
qa.e: Collateral is an asset the borrower owns, such as land, a building, a vehicle or livestock, which the lender can sell if the loan is not repaid.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT one of the terms of credit?
qa.a: The lender's favourite sport
qa.e: Terms of credit include interest rate, collateral, documentation and mode of repayment.

qa.q: Which of these is a formal source of credit?
qa.a: A cooperative society
qa.e: Banks and cooperatives are formal sources; the others are informal.

qa.q: Who supervises the functioning of formal sources of loans in India?
qa.a: The Reserve Bank of India
qa.e: The RBI monitors banks — their cash balances, whom they lend to and at what interest rate.

qa.q: Ravi borrows ₹10,000 for 12 months. A moneylender charges 5% per month; a bank charges 12% per year. How much more interest would he pay the moneylender than the bank?
Shanti borrowed from a moneylender to grow crops. The crop failed, so she sold part of her land and borrowed again to repay. What is this situation called?
qa.a: Debt trap
qa.e: When credit pushes a borrower into a situation from which recovery is very painful, it is called a debt trap.

qa.q: Why do many poor households depend on informal sources of credit?
qa.a: They often lack collateral and documents that banks ask for
qa.e: Without collateral and paperwork, the poor find bank loans hard to get, so they turn to moneylenders who know them personally.

qa.q: How many members does a typical Self-Help Group have?
qa.e: A typical SHG has 15–20 members, usually women from one neighbourhood.

qa.q: Why are banks willing to lend to SHGs even without collateral?
qa.a: Because the group as a whole takes responsibility for repayment
qa.e: The group guarantees repayment and members follow up with anyone who does not repay, so the risk for the bank is lower.

qa.q: When does an SHG usually become eligible for a bank loan?
qa.a: After a year or two of regular savings
qa.e: Banks lend once the group has shown regular saving for a year or two.

qa.q: In whose name is a bank loan to an SHG sanctioned?
qa.a: The group
qa.e: The loan is given in the group's name; the group then lends to its members.

qa.q: How does the interest charged on SHG loans compare with that of moneylenders?
qa.a: It is lower
qa.e: SHGs charge members lower interest than moneylenders do.

qa.q: Apart from loans, how do SHGs help their members?
qa.a: They make women financially self-reliant and give a platform to discuss social issues
qa.e: SHGs build women's confidence and income, and regular meetings let them discuss health, nutrition and domestic violence.

qa.q: How does a farmers' cooperative usually get a large loan from a bank?
qa.a: By using the deposits of its members as collateral
qa.e: The cooperative collects deposits from members and uses them as collateral for a bank loan, which it then lends to members.

qa.q: Who started the Grameen Bank of Bangladesh, which gives credit to the poor?
qa.a: Muhammad Yunus
qa.e: Muhammad Yunus started the Grameen Bank; he and the bank received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2006.

qa.q: What is a Multinational Corporation (MNC)?
qa.a: A company that owns or controls production in more than one nation
qa.e: An MNC's production is spread across more than one country.

qa.q: Why do MNCs set up production in countries like India?
qa.a: To get cheaper skilled labour and be close to large markets
qa.e: Low-cost skilled labour and nearness to big markets reduce costs and increase profits.

qa.q: According to the textbook, what is the most common route for MNC investment?
qa.a: Buying up local companies and then expanding production
qa.e: MNCs most often buy existing local companies, which gives them ready factories and markets.

qa.q: What is 'foreign investment'?
qa.a: Investment made by MNCs
qa.e: Investment means buying assets like land, buildings and machines; when MNCs do it, it is foreign investment.

qa.q: A large foreign brand places orders with small garment makers in Tiruppur and sells the shirts under its own name. Which way of spreading production is this?
qa.a: Placing orders for production with small producers
qa.e: The MNC does not own these units; it gets goods made by small producers and sells them under its brand.

qa.q: How can joint production with an MNC benefit a local Indian company?
qa.a: The MNC can provide money for new machines and the latest technology
qa.e: In joint production, the MNC brings additional investment, such as faster machines, and the latest technology.

qa.q: Before the middle of the 20th century, what did colonies like India mainly export?
qa.a: Raw materials and food
qa.e: Colonies exported raw materials and food and imported finished goods.

qa.q: How does foreign trade help buyers?
qa.a: It gives them a wider choice of goods beyond what is made at home
qa.e: Foreign trade brings goods from other countries, so buyers have more choice.

qa.q: What is globalisation?
qa.a: Rapid integration or interconnection between countries through trade and investment
qa.e: Globalisation links countries closely through more foreign trade and foreign investment by MNCs.

qa.q: Under globalisation, the movement of which of these between countries is still limited?
qa.a: People
qa.e: Goods, services, investment and technology move fairly freely, but countries still restrict the movement of people.

qa.q: Which development in technology has helped globalisation the most in services like call centres?
qa.a: Information and communication technology, such as the internet
qa.e: Telecommunications, computers and the internet let services be provided instantly across countries.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of a trade barrier?
qa.a: A tax on imported goods
qa.e: A tax on imports restricts trade by making foreign goods costlier.

qa.q: Why did India put barriers on foreign trade and investment after independence?
qa.a: To protect domestic producers from foreign competition
qa.e: Indian industries were just starting, so the government shielded them from strong foreign competition.

qa.q: Around which year did India remove barriers on foreign trade and investment to a large extent?
qa.e: Major changes in economic policy were made around 1991.

qa.q: What does 'liberalisation' mean?
qa.a: Removing barriers or restrictions set by the government
qa.e: Liberalisation means freeing trade and investment from government restrictions.

qa.q: What did liberalisation mean for Indian producers?
qa.a: They had to compete with foreign producers, which pushed them to improve quality
qa.e: With barriers removed, foreign goods entered India, so Indian producers faced competition and had to improve.

qa.q: What is the main aim of the World Trade Organisation (WTO)?
qa.a: To liberalise international trade
qa.e: The WTO sets rules to reduce barriers in international trade and makes sure they are followed.

qa.q: At whose initiative was the WTO started?
qa.a: Developed countries
qa.e: The WTO was set up at the initiative of developed countries.

qa.q: Why are WTO rules often said to be unfair to developing countries?
qa.a: Developed countries have kept their own trade barriers while pushing developing countries to remove theirs
qa.e: Developed countries, for example through large farm subsidies, protect their producers while developing countries are asked to open up.

qa.q: The textbook mentions that the US government gives large sums to its farmers. What is the effect on farmers in developing countries?
qa.a: They lose out, because cheap US farm products lower the prices they can get
qa.e: Subsidised US farmers can sell at very low prices, so farmers in developing countries struggle to compete.

qa.q: Which group of consumers has benefited most from globalisation in India?
qa.a: Well-off consumers, especially in cities
qa.e: Well-off urban consumers enjoy more choice, better quality and lower prices.

qa.q: According to the textbook, for how long are companies that set up units in SEZs exempt from taxes?
qa.a: 5 years
qa.e: Companies in Special Economic Zones do not pay taxes for an initial period of five years.

qa.q: What does 'fair globalisation' mean?
qa.a: It should create opportunities for all and share the benefits better
qa.e: Fair globalisation aims for everyone, including small producers and workers, to benefit.

qa.q: Which government step would help make globalisation fairer?
qa.a: Ensuring labour laws are properly implemented so workers get their rights
qa.e: Proper labour laws protect workers, which helps share the benefits of globalisation more fairly.
